Recommendations

2. Start a show around 07:00

Shows that STARTED between 07:00 and 07:59 finished on $328 typically, across 172 shows watched to the end. The worst hour, 01:00, finished on $0 (42 shows).

Every show the monitor has watched from start to finish, grouped by the hour it began. A show is credited to the hour it STARTED, and only once it has ended, so the figure is not distorted by how long a show had been running when we happened to look. Showing up at the right time is the cheapest edge there is.

What these words mean

Final total — What a show had taken at the moment it dropped off the live list. The monitor follows every show until it ends, so this is what the show made, not what it had made when somebody happened to look.

Median / typical — The middle value. Half are above, half below. Used instead of an average because one $2,000 plant would drag an average somewhere misleading.

24 of 24 hours have at least 5 finished shows, which is the fewest that makes a typical take worth comparing. Built from 7,445 shows watched from start to finish — the same shows the heading is read off, counted the same way.

† marks an hour with fewer than 5 finished shows, so its typical take is not worth comparing. Typical final take is the column to read: it is the middle show for that hour, start to finish, so it is not dragged around by one big night. Total taken is mostly a measure of how busy an hour is — more shows also means more competition for the same buyers. Made nothing counts shows that ended on zero, which is why an hour can have sales and still show a low typical take.

3. Pack it properly

The commonest complaint in this whole market is damage, and it happens at 12 of the sellers checked. Every complaint found is below.

Every complaint, pooled across all the sellers mined. One seller's problems are their own; the same problem at many sellers is the market's — and the easiest kind of advantage, because you can simply decide not to have it. It is also why packaging is the single most-praised thing buyers mention.

The seller struggling most of those mined is plantslinger — 14.6% of their reviews are 3 stars or below, averaging 4.50. Worth reading their complaints closely: their mistakes are the cheapest ones you will ever learn from.

What goes wrongTimes mentionedShare of commented reviewsSellers it happens to
damage / condition53 review(s)1.7%12 of 13
slow / no reply19 review(s)0.6%9 of 13
wrong or missing6 review(s)0.2%5 of 13
small for price2 review(s)0.1%2 of 13

Pooled across every seller whose reviews have been mined. A complaint that shows up at MANY sellers is a market problem — and an opening, because you can simply decide not to have it.

Verbatim buyer complaints are kept out of the shared copy — they name real businesses. The themes above carry the same lesson. Open the local dashboard to read them.

Market

The picture those decisions were drawn from: where the money actually landed, how crowded each search term is, and what buyers say.

What shows finished on, by category

The money shown on a running show is a total that keeps climbing, so looking once only tells you what it had made by that moment. The monitor follows shows until they end and records what they finished on. These are the honest numbers.

What these words mean

Final total — What a show had taken at the moment it dropped off the live list. The monitor follows every show until it ends, so this is what the show made, not what it had made when somebody happened to look.

Taken so far — A running total, read while the show was still on air. It only counts what the show had sold by the moment we looked, so it is always an undercount — a show caught at minute 25 of a two-hour broadcast shows a fraction of its take. Never read it as what the show made.

Money taken — What a live show has actually sold, in dollars. The platform publishes it. (An analyst would call this GMV — gross merchandise value — but it just means total sales.)

Median / typical — The middle value. Half are above, half below. Used instead of an average because one $2,000 plant would drag an average somewhere misleading.

Which numbers these are. The table below is one run — 14:24 on 11 Sep to 14:24 on 14 Sep: 1,502 shows finished, $1,412,680. The strip at the top of the page adds up every run to date, which is 7,693 shows and $6,656,569. Both are correct — they count different things, and the bigger one is not a better version of the smaller one. A single run is what the per-category typical takes below are worked out from, because mixing runs would mix different nights.

A plant show typically finishes on $608 across 635 finished shows. The other things sold on this platform — toys, collectibles, reptiles — typically finish on about $66. Plants are running roughly 9.2× the rest of the site. That is a point about the category, not about any one seller.

Sellers with 10,000+ followers typically finish on $2,926 — about 5× a typical plant show. Based on 18 finished shows. These sellers are counted again under whatever they actually sell, so this line is a slice of the table below, not another row of it.

These totals are from 14:24 on 11 Sep to 14:24 on 14 Sep, not from right now. They are the 1502 shows that finished inside that window. 34 more were still running when it ended, and none of their money is counted here. Where the market is crowded, and where it is open

The shape of the market rather than a shopping list — what kind of thing sells, where the sellers physically are, and which parts of it nobody has taken yet.

What these words mean

Top seller share — How much of a search term one single shop holds. Over about 25% and they own it; you would be fighting for scraps. It counts listings, not sales.

Median / typical — The middle value. Half are above, half below. Used instead of an average because one $2,000 plant would drag an average somewhere misleading.

Plants against everything else on the platform6.6×a plant show finishes on $570; everything else — toys, collectibles, reptiles — on $86. From 10509 plant and 17183 non-plant shows followed to the end. This is about the category, not any one seller.
Where the sellers areFL 33%of every seller we have located. Biggest single town: Apopka, FL. 52 states in all.
Sold without shipping at all42%of listings offer local pickup. Shipping is the biggest cost and the biggest complaint in this market, and this side of it avoids both.
Listings with a single photo42%of the competition. Photographs are free and entirely under a seller's control, which makes this the cheapest edge on the page.
Shipping, as a share of the plant's price38%median. It punishes cheap plants hardest: on a $15 plant the postage can cost more than the plant.

Crowding decides whether a plant is worth growing more than price does. A term with many sellers and no dominant shop has room; one where a single shop holds 40%+ means competing with an established name for every sale. The shop is linked — when one holds a term outright, the useful question is why, and that starts with looking at what else they carry. A term with fewer than five listings shows the seller count instead of a share, because 100% of one listing is not dominance.

What stands out, and how sure we are

Each card below is one thing the data said that a person would not spot by scrolling tables — a price gap between the platforms, a term one shop has taken over, stock that is not moving, somebody new turning up. They are grouped by kind and sorted by how much to trust them: Confirmed means a second independent source agreed, Likely is one clear source, Weak is shown so you can look at it, not rely on it.

What these words mean

Confirmed / Likely / Weak — How much to trust a finding. Confirmed means a second independent source agreed — the other platform, or another day. Likely is one clear source. Weak is shown so you can look, not so you can rely on it.

Spread — The gap between the cheapest and dearest seller of the same plant. A big spread means the market has not settled on a price, which is where room usually is.

Named cultivar — A listing naming a specific variety, not just a genus — "Anthurium warocqueanum" rather than "anthurium". Used to check whether two platforms are really selling the same thing before calling a price gap arbitrage.

Same plant, different price on each platform6

The two platforms are independent sources, so when both agree a gap is real it is the strongest kind of finding here. Each one has already been checked for whether the two sides are selling the same KIND of plant.

Confirmed
"anthurium" costs 175% more on Palmstreet than Whatnot
Palmstreet $55 vs Whatnot $20. WORTH A LOOK: the cheaper side is the one with the rarer plants — 92% of Whatnot listings carry a named cultivar against 68% on Palmstreet. So Palmstreet is charging more for a plainer mix. Either Palmstreet buyers pay a premium for the platform, or Whatnot is underpricing genuinely rare stock.

How the two platforms compare1

Likely
The two platforms are different crowds — 0 of 45 sellers appear on both
63 Palmstreet sellers and 45 Whatnot sellers seen so far, with no names in common. Being on both looks like reaching two separate audiences rather than the same one twice — and almost nobody is doing it. Caveat: matched on normalised display names, so a seller trading under different names on each platform would be counted twice and missed here.
1 file this came from
seller collections, both platforms
What we did about itQueued a fresh seller scan on both sides. Name matching is the weak point here — someone trading under a different handle on each platform would be counted twice — so this keeps widening the sample rather than settling on a number too early.

What buyers bring up are themes, not word counts — each is a readable list of phrases, and the red ones are what costs sales. Reviews/day is the closest thing to a sales rate either platform exposes — only a buyer can leave a review, and unlike a raw total it compares a three-year-old shop against a new one fairly. The small number after it is the window it was measured over, and it matters: a rate off a fortnight is a guess about a year, and the two used to be printed identically. The words column is buyer vocabulary, where listing language and new plant names come from. Critical reviews are where sellers lose people.

The full write-up

More of what the numbers add up to, still in plain English.

Live selling is where the money is. At the last full snapshot, taken 17 days ago, 19 shows were broadcasting and had taken $6,039 between them. Rare plants was 48% of that, with a mid-show total of $140 apiece. Those are running totals caught mid-broadcast, not final takings — what shows actually finish on is in What shows finished on, by category. It is also why the sellers in Your competitors who run no live shows stand out.

468 plant names were found by reading real listings — nobody typed them into a search box. 36 of them sell at three figures or more. The dearest: anthurium pallidiflorum at $250, anthurium panamense at $250, alocasia mystery box at $220. 18 of the 36 priciest are anthuriums, which is the clearest steer here: that is where the money concentrates.

Where there is room, and where there is not. “alocasia black velvet” is the most open — 98 different sellers and the biggest holds only 3%, so nobody owns it; “alocasia variegated black” is already taken — one seller holds 100% of it. Crowding matters more than price: a dear plant nobody can reach is worth less than a cheaper one you can actually sell.

14 finding(s) are corroborated by both platforms independently — those are the ones to act on first. The rest come from a single source and are marked as such. Nothing here is an estimate.

Everything above is generated from the data in the tables on this page — if a number moves, this moves with it.

What these words mean

Median / typical — The middle value. Half are above, half below. Used instead of an average because one $2,000 plant would drag an average somewhere misleading.

Spread — The gap between the cheapest and dearest seller of the same plant. A big spread means the market has not settled on a price, which is where room usually is.

Every row was searched by name, so the seller count is real. Still scarce is the window worth propagating into: enough people want it to prove demand, not enough can supply it. Supply flooding in means new stock is arriving faster than the market can absorb, which is what the months before a price collapse look like. Shipping as % of price is the quiet killer: past about half, postage costs more than the margin.
Read a suspiciously cheap row twice. A search matches text, so a famously rare plant showing a low price usually means it matched seedlings, cuttings or unrelated listings rather than the plant itself — the price is real, what it is the price OF may not be.

Search terms — what each is worth, and who is already there

For each phrase someone might search: what it sells for, how many sellers are posting under it, how much of that posting one shop accounts for, and where the listings actually cluster by price. A shop posting most of the listings is not the same as owning the market — it counts listings, not sales.

What these words mean

Top seller share — How much of a search term one single shop holds. Over about 25% and they own it; you would be fighting for scraps. It counts listings, not sales.

Median / typical — The middle value. Half are above, half below. Used instead of an average because one $2,000 plant would drag an average somewhere misleading.

In niche = how many of this seller's listings turned up in the searches we ran (anthurium, variegated, philodendron, monstera, alocasia, hoya) — a sample of their presence there, not their whole shop. Hover any number for its definition. Seller names link to their page — open one and look before acting on a row. Sales counts are published by the platforms, not estimated. big = top decile by sales · no shows = sells well but is not doing live, which is where the money is · premium = median $100+ · new = no sales yet.

The shops that hold a plant to themselves

When one shop is the only seller of a plant, the useful question is why. This is what those shops are, in their own words.

What these words mean

Named cultivar — A listing naming a specific variety, not just a genus — "Anthurium warocqueanum" rather than "anthurium". Used to check whether two platforms are really selling the same thing before calling a price gap arbitrage.

ShopLifetime salesTerms it topsSole source ofListings shown vs heldWhat it is
EcuageneraFL →61,8227—6,546 shown of 19,950“Aroids, orchids, tropical plants & more!”
GayPlantHeaux →7933—on Instagram “instagram @GAYPLANTHEAUX”
plantamani →—2——nothing published beyond the storefront

Sole source of counts the terms where this shop is the ONLY seller. That is the interesting column: a shop with tens of thousands of sales holding ground is ordinary scale, but a shop with a few dozen sales that is the only source of three named cultivars has material nobody else can get — and those need completely different responses. Listings shown vs held is how much inventory is not on display. Everything in the last column is what the business publishes about itself.

About this data

How this was collected

The method behind every number above — the sources, the window, the sample sizes, and what this data cannot tell you. (If you have seen a research report before, this is the methodology section.)

Where the numbers come from

Two live-selling platforms, Palmstreet and Whatnot, read directly from what they publish. Nothing here is a survey, a panel or an estimate: every figure is a count of something that was on one of those two sites at a stated moment. Where a number could not be measured it is left out rather than filled in.

When

Collected on 18 days between 4 Sep 2026 and 22 Sep 2026, across 432 saved files. The two halves are not equally fresh and the strip at the top of the page says which is which — live shows are re-read every few minutes, prices and sellers only when a collection is run.

Sample size

What was measuredHow manyWhat it counts
Listing readings102,191Every listing read, on every pass. Reading the same listing on two days counts twice.
Reviews read4,392Buyer reviews mined from seller pages, for the complaint and vocabulary work.
Live shows watched37,971Shows the monitor followed. Not all of them finished while it was watching.
Shows watched to the end7,693The only ones whose takings are final. Every other money figure is a mid-show snapshot and an undercount.
Distinct plant names468Read out of what people are actually selling, not typed in by us.
Distinct sellers338Across both platforms.

These are READINGS, not distinct items. The stored total is small because the collectors keep measurements and throw the material away: a run reads hundreds of listings, records the counts, prices and locations, and discards every title and description.

Limitations — what this cannot tell you

  • These are floors, not censuses. Palmstreet serves live shows through a personalised 'for_you' feed -- every record carries section=for_you and there is no per-category live URL (five tried, all 404). So these counts are a FLOOR, not a census: they are what the feed shows an anonymous visitor, which may not be every show on the platform.
  • Listings are not sales. A shop posting most of the listings under a term holds the shelf space, not necessarily the revenue. Only the finished-show figures are money that changed hands.
  • A search matches text. A famously rare plant showing a low price usually means the search caught seedlings, cuttings or unrelated listings rather than the plant itself. Read a suspiciously cheap row twice.
  • Thin cells are marked, not hidden. A dagger means fewer than 10 finished shows behind a category, or fewer than 5 behind an hour. A trend line needs 4 readings before it is drawn at all; below that the reading count is shown instead.
  • One week is not a season. Nothing here can tell you whether a price is high for the year or high for this fortnight. That needs the collection to keep running, which is the cheapest thing on this list.
